Unit 01 — Reading the Scoreboard: Revenue, Profit & Margin

6 min read1,370 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06learn/unit-01-reading-the-scoreboard.md
On this page

  2. ① Material — what we're learning, and where it lives

For a complete beginner. No prior business knowledge assumed. By the end you'll be able to look at a company and answer the first question that matters: did it actually make money — and how much of each dollar did it keep? The four pillars are labeled so you can see how this is taught.

Plain words first (terms we use in passing — read once)

  • $X B — X billion dollars.
  • Net income — just another name for profit: what's left after all costs ("net" = after everything).
  • Debt — money the company borrowed and must pay back, usually with interest.
  • Fixed costs — bills that don't shrink when sales fall (rent, loan payments, salaried crew).
  • Public company — a company whose shares anyone can buy on a stock market; in exchange it must publish its finances. (A private company doesn't and can keep them secret.)
  • 10-K — the detailed annual report every U.S. public company must file with the government.
  • SEC / EDGAR — the SEC is the U.S. agency that regulates public companies; EDGAR is its free public website where every filing lives.
  • Fiscal year — a company's official 12-month accounting year (often, not always, Jan–Dec).
  • Second-order effect — the knock-on consequence: what happens next, after the obvious first effect.

(Revenue, profit, and margin are the lesson itself — taught below.)

① Material — what we're learning, and where it lives

Every company keeps a scoreboard called the income statement (you'll also hear "P&L" — profit and loss). It answers one question: over some period, did the business make money? It has three core ideas, and that's all this unit covers:

  • Revenue — all the money customers paid the company.
  • Costs — everything it spent to earn that revenue.
  • Profit (a.k.a. net income) — what's left: Revenue − Costs.

Where it comes from: every U.S. public company files this with the government every year, in a document called a 10-K, free at SEC EDGAR. We'll read a real one below. (Go deeper later: lessons/core-01-accounting.html, and the worked Apple example in notes/01-accounting.)

② Understanding — the idea in plain language

Picture a lemonade stand. - Customers pay you $100 over the summer → that's revenue. - Lemons, sugar, cups cost $70 → those are costs. - You keep $30 → that's profit.

Three things a beginner must internalize:

1. Revenue is not profit. Revenue is the top line (money in the door). Profit is the bottom line (what survives after costs). A company can have huge revenue and still lose money if its costs are higher. People who only watch revenue get fooled constantly.

2. Margin is the number that actually tells you something. Net margin = profit ÷ revenue — how many cents of each $1 of sales the company keeps. (It comes out as a decimal; multiply by 100 to make it a percent — e.g. 0.17 = 17%. "17%" and "17 cents of profit per dollar of sales" are the same thing.)

Stand A: $1,000,000 revenue, keeps $50,000 → 5% margin. Stand B: $200,000 revenue, keeps $80,000 → 40% margin. Stand B is the better business, even though Stand A's headline is 5× bigger. Margin > headline.

3. Some costs don't shrink when sales fall. The lemonade stand's lemons scale with sales — sell nothing, buy no lemons. But if you signed a year's rent on the stand, that bill comes whether you sell one cup or a thousand. Those are fixed costs, and they're why a bad year can turn brutal: revenue falls, but the big bills stay. Hold that thought — the real example shows it vividly.

③ Example — real company, real event (the part a textbook can't do)

Meet Royal Caribbean Cruises — the cruise-ship company. Here are its actual numbers, pulled from its SEC filings (all figures real, in USD):

Fiscal year Revenue Profit (net income) Net margin What was happening
2019 $10.95 B +$1.88 B ~17% A normal year — ships full, sailing.
2020 $2.21 B −$5.80 B ≈ −262% COVID-19. Cruising was ordered to stop (no-sail orders, ~March 2020).
2022 $8.84 B −$2.16 B ≈ −24% Sailing resumed; recovering — but not all the way.

Read what this teaches, in order:

  • 2019 — the baseline (the "normal" year to compare against). For every $1 of tickets, Royal Caribbean kept about 17¢ of profit (a 17% net margin). Notice revenue ($10.95B) and profit ($1.88B) are very different numbers — revenue ≠ profit, exactly as we said above.
  • 2020 — the event hits. The pandemic (cruising was literally ordered to halt) erased the customers. Revenue collapsed ~80%, from $10.95B to $2.21B. Here the real filing shows the number and the real event explains the why — that pairing is the whole point of using a real company.
  • A margin can go below zero — far below. 2020's net margin was ≈ −262%: −$5.80B loss ÷ $2.21B revenue ≈ −2.62. How do you "lose 262% of sales"? Because costs ran far past revenue — costs must have been about $8B (the $2.2B taken in plus the $5.8B lost), so the loss is bigger than everything you sold. Margin is just profit ÷ revenue; when profit is a big negative, the percentage can exceed 100%.
  • The brutal part — fixed costs. That loss was a ~$7.7B swing from 2019's profit (the gap from a +$1.88B profit to a −$5.80B loss is the two added together: 1.88 + 5.80 ≈ 7.7). Why so much worse than the 80% revenue drop? Because ships, crews, and debt payments (money borrowed for the ships) don't disappear when the boats stop — those fixed costs kept billing, turning a revenue drop into a catastrophic loss. This is why the cruise lines nearly didn't survive.
  • 2022 — the second-order lesson. Revenue recovered to $8.84B (~81% of 2019) — but they still lost money (−$2.16B). Take-away a beginner should carry forever: "sales came back" is not the same as "the business is healthy again." Profit lags revenue. Watch the bottom line, not just the top.

That's the whole differentiator: you didn't learn "margin" from a definition — you watched it happen to a real $10-billion company during an event you already understand.

④ Application — your turn (small and doable)

A. Compute (2 min). Royal Caribbean 2019: profit $1.88B on revenue $10.95B. What's the net margin? (Answer: 1.88 ÷ 10.95 ≈ 0.17, and 0.17 × 100 = 17%.)

B. Explain in one sentence. In 2020 Royal Caribbean still took in $2.2B of revenue but lost $5.8B. Why was the loss so much bigger than the revenue drop? (You're right if you said: its big fixed costs — ships, crew, debt — kept billing even though sailings stopped.)

C. One more margin (no computer needed). Apple in a recent year earned about $97B of profit on $383B of revenue. Estimate its net margin, and say whether Apple keeps more or less of each sales dollar than Royal Caribbean did in 2019 (17%). (≈ 97 ÷ 383 ≈ 0.25 = 25% — Apple keeps more.)

D. Optional — pull it yourself (only if you have this project set up). If you've got the repo running, you can fetch any company's real numbers: python3 _ingest/edgar.py facts AAPL. No setup? Skip it — you've already done the core skill in A–C.

Check yourself

  1. A company reports $5B in revenue and a $400M loss. Did it make money? (No — profit is negative; revenue ≠ profit.)
  2. Company X: $50M profit on $1B revenue. Company Y: $50M profit on $200M revenue. Which is the stronger business? (Y — 25% margin vs X's 5%.)
  3. Why can a company's revenue recover after a shock while it's still unprofitable? (Costs — especially fixed ones, and debt taken on to survive — can stay high even as sales return.)
